result.text: The paper tackles multi-hop reasoning over incomplete knowledge graphs, where existing RL-based path-finding agents treat entity/relation embeddings as deterministic points and suffer from premature exploitation due to biased policy gradients. Its key insight is to model representations and Q-values probabilistically so that uncertainty guides exploration, enabling the agent to consider regions of the state space rather than overcommitting to high-reward paths. Methodologically, the authors propose GaussianPath, a Bayesian Q-learning framework that initializes representation layers with Gaussian (or pre-trained) priors and learns a state-action value function under uncertainty to regularize training and encourage broader exploration. Experiments on multiple KGs demonstrate that this uncertainty-aware approach yields superior performance to deterministic baselines, particularly on automatically extracted graphs.

The paper addresses shortcomings in 3D scene understanding by large language models—specifically poor object-level referencing and grounding across diverse scene-language tasks. Its key insight is to represent a 3D scene as an explicit sequence of object-centric embeddings each paired with a unique identifier token, which converts spatial grounding into token-level reference that a language model can reliably attend to. The method decomposes scenes into object proposals, extracts semantic-rich 2D/3D embeddings for each object, attaches identifier tokens, and formulates all downstream tasks as unified QA over these identifiers so the same LLM head can jointly learn grounding and language tasks with minimal fine-tuning. This object-identifier paradigm yields strong gains on multiple benchmarks (ScanRefer, Multi3DRefer, Scan2Cap, ScanQA, SQA3D) by improving general referencing, grounding, and multi-task training efficiency.

The paper addresses the problem that safety-aligned large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and that existing safeguard approaches—especially using the model to self-classify harmful prompts—suffer from poor detection due to a domain shift between the model’s trained self-censoring behavior and the classification task. The key insight is that asking the model to repeat its own outputs preserves the model’s natural alignment behavior and avoids the domain shift introduced by explicit classification, improving discrimination between safe and malicious responses without requiring fine-tuning or white-box access. The authors propose PARDEN, a lightweight safeguard that simply prompts the model to regenerate or repeat candidate outputs and then applies detection on the repeated text; empirical results on Llama-2 and Claude-2 show PARDEN substantially reduces false positives at high true-positive rates (e.g., an ~11× FPR reduction for Llama2-7B at 90% TPR) compared to baseline jailbreak detectors.

The paper addresses limitations of visual prompt tuning (VPT)—notably poor initialization, sensitivity to prompt length, and weak performance when adapting self-supervised pretrained vision models to downstream tasks—and seeks a lightweight way to boost adaptation without full fine-tuning. The key insight is that learned prompt tokens rapidly become highly correlated with downstream image patch tokens, so initializing prompts from downstream token prototypes (clusters of target-token features) gives a strong, semantically meaningful starting point that improves mutual information with patches. Methodologically, the authors propose Self-Prompt-Tuning (SPT): compute prototype tokens from downstream data, initialize and optionally refine a small set of learnable prompt tokens based on these prototypes, and use a streamlined optimization pipeline that keeps compute overhead negligible compared to VPT; extensive experiments show SPT outperforms prior prompt and full fine-tuning on many benchmarks while using <0.4% of parameters and substantially improves adaptation for self-supervised pretrained models.

The paper addresses the lack of large-scale, egocentric datasets that combine accurate 3D camera geometry with annotated video understanding for neural rendering and dynamic scene modeling. Its key insight is that augmenting an existing action-rich egocentric video corpus (EPIC-KITCHENS) with reconstructed camera poses and geometry removes the costly photogrammetry bottleneck and better supports tasks that require both spatial structure and semantic labels. The authors introduce EPIC Fields, a dataset that registers 19M frames across 45 kitchens (recovering cameras for 96% of videos) and pairs these 3D-enabled videos with action segments and VISOR object masks, and they demonstrate the utility by proposing methods and strong baselines for neural rendering and dynamic object segmentation that reveal current limitations and show geometry improves semi-supervised segmentation.

The paper addresses the lack of consensus and conversion difficulty between LayerNorm (LN) and RMSNorm in Transformer architectures, where RMSNorm is cheaper but thought to reduce representational power compared to LN. The key insight is that the mean component removed by Pre-LN is redundant in the main residual branch, so by explicitly compressing or eliminating this zero-mean information one can reduce LN to an RMS-style normalization without loss of arithmetic functionality. The authors introduce Compressed RMSNorm (CRMSNorm) and corresponding Pre-CRMSNorm Transformers that perform a lossless compression of zero-mean vectors and prove formal equivalence between Pre-LN, Pre-RMSNorm, and Pre-CRMSNorm during training and inference, enabling direct substitution. Empirically, replacing Pre-LN with Pre-(C)RMSNorm yields identical behavior while cutting training and inference time by about 1%–10%.

The paper addresses the problem of learning near-optimal predictive models when deploying a model changes the data distribution (performative prediction) and the learner must both collect feedback and minimize cumulative regret. The key insight is that performative feedback—observing samples from the induced shifted distribution after each deployment—yields a richer signal than standard bandit feedback, allowing regret to scale with the complexity of distribution shifts rather than the complexity of the reward function. The authors propose an algorithm that, under only smoothness assumptions on the shifts (no convexity needed), carefully explores to learn the mapping from models to induced distributions and constructs novel confidence bounds on unexplored models’ risks; this yields regret guarantees and ensures the final iterate is near-optimal. More broadly, their approach adapts bandit-style tools to exploit performative feedback for efficient regret minimization.

The paper addresses understanding and extending the transformer attention mechanism by linking it to associative memory: it asks what kind of memory model attention implements and how that explains transformers’ behavior and learning. The key insight is that transformer attention is exactly the update rule of a newly formulated modern Hopfield network with continuous states that can store an exponential number of patterns, converge rapidly (often in one update), and trade off storage capacity against convergence speed and retrieval error; this interpretation explains three types of energy minima (global averaging, metastable subset-averaging, and single-pattern fixed points) and how different transformer layers and attention heads operate and learn. Methodologically, the authors derive the Hopfield energy and update equations that match attention, analyze dynamics and gradients across layers (showing early layers favor global averaging while later layers form metastable attractors), demonstrate practical gains on tasks like immune-repertoire classification, and provide a PyTorch "Hopfield" layer and Gaussian-weighting simplification for replacing average-like heads to integrate this memory-attention perspective into deep architectures.

The paper tackles the problem of improving data efficiency in deep reinforcement learning by leveraging unlabeled observational data to pretrain encoders that can be finetuned with minimal task interaction. The key insight is that representations which jointly capture latent dynamics and afford goal-conditioned behavioral structure generalize better for downstream RL with limited on-policy data. The method combines latent dynamics modeling with unsupervised goal-conditioned RL to pretrain an encoder from diverse, task-aligned observations, then finetunes this encoder with only 100k environment steps on Atari, showing strong gains over prior offline-pretraining baselines and competitive performance with much larger pretraining regimes. The approach scales favorably with larger models and more diverse observational data, approaching human-level performance and data-efficiency in the best settings.

The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection, aiming to transfer detector performance from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain while avoiding negative transfer from imperfect feature alignment. Its key insight is that learning category-specific dictionaries from source-domain object proposals lets target proposals be represented per-category, and the reconstruction residuals provide a reliable signal both for assigning pseudo-labels and estimating box quality (e.g., IoU), avoiding reliance on brittle global feature alignment or softmax decision boundaries. The method builds category dictionaries from source proposals, computes residuals for target candidate boxes to guide pseudo-box selection and weight their contribution by residual-derived quality scores, and trains the detector in a residual-weighted self-training loop that implicitly aligns domains and yields more informative, trustworthy pseudo-labels for improved cross-domain detection.

result.text: Ferret tackles the problem of precise spatial referring and open-vocabulary grounding in images, enabling multimodal models to refer to and describe regions of any shape or granularity while avoiding object hallucination. The key insight is a hybrid region representation that jointly encodes discrete coordinates and continuous visual features, combined with a spatial-aware visual sampler that can extract informative continuous features from arbitrarily shaped, sparse regions. Ferret’s method unifies referring and grounding in an LLM by accepting diverse region inputs (points, boxes, free-form shapes), training on a large curated GRIT dataset of 1.1M refer-and-ground instruction samples (including 95K hard negatives), and fine-tuning the multimodal LLM to reason and respond about region-based queries; this yields state-of-the-art performance on classical referring/grounding tasks and markedly better region-based multimodal dialogue and localization.

result.text: The paper tackles synthesizing free-viewpoint video of arbitrary human performances from sparse multi-view cameras, where prior NeRF-based methods either overfit to a single person or fail to generalize to humans because of heavy occlusions and complex articulations. The key insight is to combine a parametric human body model with temporal and multi-view attention mechanisms so that tracked skeletal motion guides robust aggregation of visual evidence across time and views, enabling generalization to unseen identities and poses. Concretely, Neural Human Performer first uses a temporal transformer to fuse tracked, body-aligned features over time according to skeletal motion, then applies a multi-view transformer that cross-attends between these temporally-fused features and pixel-aligned features from each camera at each timestep to integrate multi-view observations on the fly and predict radiance fields. Experiments on ZJU-MoCap and AIST demonstrate substantial improvements over recent generalizable NeRF approaches for novel humans and poses.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised cross-domain object detection, where detectors trained on a source domain fail on a target domain due to biased, batch-based semantic estimates and class-agnostic alignment that scrambles class-specific distributions. The key insight is to build an unbiased, aggregated semantic paradigm from class-specific semantics across source images and use it to condition adaptation so that alignment is both class-aware and robust to sampling bias. The method constructs a graph-aggregated semantic paradigm that a lightweight module turns into conditional kernels to extract target semantics, integrates these kernels into a Conditional Kernel guided Alignment (CKA) for class-specific global alignment, and transfers paradigm knowledge via a Graph-based Semantic Transfer (GST) into the target category feature space, yielding significantly improved domain-adaptive detection.

The paper tackles few-shot reinforcement learning where each task is governed by an unknown subtask graph specifying subtasks and their dependencies, and the agent must rapidly adapt across a few episodes to maximize test-phase return. The key insight is to meta-learn an inference procedure for the latent subtask-graph parameter rather than a fixed meta-policy, enabling the agent to identify task structure on the fly and then act optimally conditioned on that inferred structure. The proposed method, Meta-learner with Subtask Graph Inference (MSGI), interleaves interaction-driven posterior inference over latent graph parameters with a policy conditioned on those parameters, and it augments training with an intrinsic exploration bonus inspired by upper confidence bound to drive efficient discovery of dependencies. Empirically on grid-worlds and StarCraft II scenarios, MSGI more accurately recovers latent task parameters and adapts faster than baseline meta-RL and hierarchical RL approaches.

result.text: The paper investigates whether safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) holds when users communicate in non-natural languages (ciphers), addressing the risk that current defenses—trained primarily on natural language—may be bypassed. The key insight is that LLMs can understand and respond to ciphered prompts, and in fact exhibit a latent "secret cipher" behavior that can be triggered via role play and enciphered demonstrations, enabling stealthy jailbreaks even against strong models like GPT-4. The authors introduce CipherChat, a framework that sends system-role descriptions and few-shot enciphered examples to LLMs to systematically evaluate 11 safety domains across English and Chinese, showing that many human-designed ciphers and the proposed SelfCipher can nearly completely bypass GPT-4’s safety in several domains. Their results reveal a pressing need to extend alignment methods beyond natural languages and provide code and data for reproducibility.

result.text: The paper tackles efficient compression of Transformer models for resource-constrained deployment, noting that prior weight-focused low-rank approximations perform poorly for transformers and require large labeled datasets to fine-tune. Its key insight is that activations (features) in transformer layers are empirically low-rank even though the learned weight matrices are not, so compressing outputs rather than weights yields more faithful reduction. result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised monocular depth estimation in dynamic scenes by explicitly modeling per-object 6-DoF motion together with camera ego-motion, addressing failures of prior methods that treat moving objects as outliers. Its key insight is that correctly handling object motion requires a geometrically accurate forward-projection formulation (not the common inverse projection) and that combining instance-aware photometric and geometric consistency yields stronger self-supervision for both background and object regions. The method implements a neural forward-projection module to render objects under estimated 6-DoF transforms, integrates a unified instance-aware consistency loss that enforces photometric and geometric alignment for each segmented instance, and leverages an auto-annotation pipeline using off-the-shelf instance segmentation and optical flow to produce video instance masks for training. Empirically, this end-to-end framework improves depth and motion estimation on KITTI and Cityscapes, outperforming prior state-of-the-art approaches.

The key insight is a theoretically motivated policy similarity metric (PSM) that rates states as similar when the optimal policies at those states — and in their future trajectories — are alike, thereby encoding sequential and long-horizon behavioral equivalence rather than superficial observation similarity. result.text: The paper addresses exploration-exploitation in continuous-state-action reinforcement learning by providing theoretical guarantees and a practical algorithm for model-based posterior sampling. The paper tackles the practical challenge of reducing Transformer inference cost without the high time and complexity of retraining-based pruning methods by proposing a fast post-training pruning framework. The key insight is that structured sparsity can be applied post-training if one carefully selects and adjusts masks to preserve important parameters—using Fisher-information-guided mask search, complementary mask rearrangement, and a lightweight mask-tuning step that reconstructs layer outputs. Their method automatically finds which heads and filters to remove under a resource constraint and applies only brief, layerwise reconstruction (no full retraining), enabling up to 2.0x FLOPs reduction and 1.56x latency speedup on BERT-base and DistilBERT with under 1% accuracy loss on GLUE and SQuAD. Crucially, the entire procedure runs in under three minutes on a single GPU, offering a practical, two-orders-of-magnitude faster alternative to retraining-based pruning.

result.text: The paper tackles safe exploration in episodic constrained Markov decision processes, asking whether one can obtain near-optimal reward regret while eliminating or sharply limiting constraint violations. Its key insight is that combining optimism for reward with pessimism for constraints—leveraging a known strictly safe baseline when available or conservatively estimating constraint costs otherwise—lets an agent explore without incurring growing safety breaches. Concretely, when a strictly safe policy is known the authors design an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that confines constraint violation to zero with high probability while maintaining Õ(√K) reward regret; when no safe policy is known but one exists, they give a primal–dual method that uses optimistic primal estimates and pessimistic dual updates to guarantee only bounded constraint violation with high probability alongside Õ(√K) regret.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of learning goal-conditioned policies from diverse offline (reward-free) datasets, where estimating exact value for distant goals is unreliable and long-horizon goal-reaching is difficult. The key insight is that goal-reaching naturally decomposes hierarchically—reaching far goals requires passing through nearer subgoals whose values are easier to estimate—so treating intermediate states as latent “actions” lets a high-level policy propose subgoals while a low-level policy executes to them, reducing reliance on accurate long-horizon value estimates. The method, HIQL, learns a single action-free value function and two policies from offline data: a high-level policy that predicts a latent representation of a subgoal (treating states as actions) and a low-level policy that outputs primitive actions to reach that subgoal; this hierarchical decomposition is shown analytically and empirically to be robust to value estimation noise and effective on long-horizon and image-based offline goal-reaching tasks, including leveraging action-free data.

The key insight is that combining a mean-teacher two-stage pipeline with masked feature alignment and a target-like pretraining set yields more robust and consistent adaptation: masked alignment reduces harmful domain interference, target-like pretraining stabilizes learning, and object-query knowledge transfer preserves student gains. The method (MTM) first pretrains the detector on labeled, style-transferred target-like images to avoid fluctuation, then self-trains with mean-teacher pseudo-labels while applying Object Queries Knowledge Transfer (OQKT) and two complementary masked feature alignment modules—Masked Domain Query-based Feature Alignment (MDQFA) and Masked Token-wise Feature Alignment (MTWFA)—to align features selectively and prevent training stagnation, with experiments and theory showing improved robustness across scenarios.

result.text: Extend object-identifier LLM grounding in 3D to a persistent 4D setting where the same real-world instance keeps a stable token across multiple scans of a scene. We learn a cross-scan object codebook by aligning instances with a contrastive tracking objective while distilling synthetic multi-view 2D cues into the 3D encoder and injecting motion-aware pairwise geometry into attention, so the LLM can answer temporal referring and change-centric questions. Each identifier token carries lightweight temporal slots (pose/appearance deltas and relation edges) that let the model attend over changes instead of re-detecting. Supervision is bootstrapped from hierarchical region–object annotations by generating pseudo-temporal pairs via partial rescans and scene perturbations with change-focused language prompts, enabling capabilities like “find the chair that moved since yesterday” without a dedicated tracking head.

result.text: The paper examines the overlooked safety risks that arise when end-users fine-tune already-aligned large language models (LLMs), showing that custom fine-tuning can undo alignment even without malicious intent. Its key insight is that small amounts of adversarial or even benign training data can substantially weaken safety guardrails—e.g., jailbreaking GPT-3.5 Turbo with just 10 adversarial examples via inexpensive API fine-tuning—so initial alignment does not guarantee post-tuning safety. The authors demonstrate this through red-teaming experiments that fine-tune models on crafted and common datasets and measure increased responsiveness to harmful instructions, and they analyze why existing inference-time safety infrastructures fail to prevent these post-tuning vulnerabilities. They conclude by evaluating mitigation strategies (policy, access controls, detection, robust fine-tuning techniques) and call for focused research and stricter safety protocols governing who may fine-tune aligned models and how.

result.text: The paper addresses the understudied problem of calibrating deep neural network object detectors, especially under domain shift where miscalibration can harm downstream decisions. Its key insight is that calibration for detection requires both a train-time, task-aware loss that directly encourages probability-confidence alignment for detection outputs and an uncertainty-aware mechanism during self-training to implicitly reduce calibration errors when adapting to new domains. The authors introduce TCD, a plug-and-play auxiliary calibration loss that integrates with standard detection objectives to improve confidence reliability, and an implicit calibration method for domain-adaptive self-training that quantifies detection uncertainty to guide pseudo-labeling; experiments show these complementary techniques substantially improve calibration for multiple detectors in both in-domain and out-of-domain adaptation scenarios.

result.text: The paper investigates how pre-trained language models acquire multi-step reasoning ability from next-token prediction by proposing that LMs aggregate indirect reasoning paths observed during pre-training. The key insight is that reasoning can be modeled as a weighted aggregation of random-walk paths on knowledge or reasoning graphs, so the LM’s output distribution effectively sums probabilities of relevant path-derived conclusions. To test this, the authors formalize reasoning paths as random walks over knowledge graphs and chain-of-thought graphs, analyze learned LM distributions to show alignment with weighted random-walk probabilities, and demonstrate empirically across KG and CoT datasets that training with (and augmenting) unlabeled random-walk reasoning paths improves multi-step reasoning performance.

result.text: The paper addresses how Transformers perform in-context learning, seeking a mechanistic explanation for how autoregressively trained models can learn new tasks from input/output examples without weight updates. The key insight is that a single linear self-attention layer can implement the same data transformation as one step of gradient descent on a regression loss, and that when Transformers are trained on regression tasks they either reproduce gradient-descent solutions or converge to weights matching this constructive mapping, effectively becoming mesa-optimizers that perform gradient descent in their forward pass. Methodologically, the authors provide an explicit weight construction proving the equivalence between linear attention and a GD update, then empirically train self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression problems to show similarity between Transformer inference and iterative GD (including learned curvature corrections and learning linear models on deep representations for nonlinear tasks), and relate these findings to previously identified induction-head mechanisms.

args.text: Visual prompt tuning still lacks spatial selectivity, causing object and context evidence to tangle and degrade transfer under domain shift and fine-grained recognition. I propose Region-Conditioned Prototype Prompting (RCPP): use off-the-shelf segmentation masks to partition tokens into foreground and context, compute region-specific token prototypes on downstream data, and initialize two small prompt banks from these prototypes—foreground prompts injected in early layers to modulate masked patches and context prompts injected in mid/late layers to capture background priors (building on prototype-based initialization). Training enforces disentanglement via an orthogonality constraint between the two banks and balances their mutual information with masked vs. unmasked tokens; at inference, per-image sparse routing selects a few prompts from each bank by cross-attention on the current masks for fast, test-time adaptation. Applied to self-supervised ViTs and CLIP-style VLMs, RCPP should improve few-shot and cross-domain performance by combining mask-driven fine-grained prompting with lightweight, per-sample adaptation and concept alignment.

result.text: The paper tackles slow inference in diffusion transformers, where each denoising step executes a large transformer resulting in high computational cost. result.text: The paper addresses understanding and extending the transformer attention mechanism by linking it to associative memory: it asks what kind of memory model attention implements and how that explains transformers’ behavior and learning. The key insight is that transformer attention is exactly the update rule of a newly formulated modern Hopfield network with continuous states that can store an exponential number of patterns, converge rapidly (often in one update), and trade off storage capacity against convergence speed and retrieval error; this interpretation explains three types of energy minima (global averaging, metastable subset-averaging, and single-pattern fixed points) and how different transformer layers and attention heads operate and learn. Methodologically, the authors derive the Hopfield energy and update equations that match attention, analyze dynamics and gradients across layers (showing early layers favor global averaging while later layers form metastable attractors), demonstrate practical gains on tasks like immune-repertoire classification, and provide a PyTorch "Hopfield" layer and Gaussian-weighting simplification for replacing average-like heads to integrate this memory-attention perspective into deep architectures.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of answering complex multi-hop first-order logic (FOL) queries over large, incomplete knowledge graphs, where prior embedding-based methods are limited to subsets of FOL (typically conjunctions) and cannot model negation or uncertainty. The key insight is to represent entities and queries as probabilistic embeddings with bounded support—specifically Beta distributions—so that logical operators can be expressed as neural operators acting on these distributions, enabling faithful handling of conjunction, disjunction, and negation while capturing uncertainty. The method, called BetaE, embeds entities/queries as Beta distributions in latent space and learns neural projection, intersection, union, and complement operators to perform logical reasoning in that space, and it is evaluated on three large KGs where it outperforms previous methods (including up to 25.4% relative improvement) while supporting arbitrary FOL queries.

The paper addresses the challenge of open-vocabulary 3D scene segmentation where large-scale labeled 3D datasets are lacking and existing 2D open-vocabulary models often lose generality after finetuning on closed vocabularies. Its key insight is that pre-trained multimodal foundation models (CLIP for language–image alignment and DINO for self-supervised visual features) can be weakly distilled into a 3D representation without any manual segmentation labels by leveraging only scene text descriptions, thereby preserving open-vocabulary capabilities while imposing 3D view consistency. The method embeds CLIP and DINO features into a neural radiance field (NeRF) and trains the NeRF to reproduce those 2D multimodal and object-centric cues across views, yielding a view-consistent 3D feature field that supports open-vocabulary segmentation via text queries. Experiments show this weakly supervised distillation can match or even surpass some fully supervised 3D segmentation models, indicating that 3D open-vocabulary understanding can be learned effectively from 2D images and text–image pairs.

args.text: We propose Energy-Steered In-Context Learning (ES-ICL), a transformer layer that treats attention as a modern Hopfield update and explicitly shapes its energy to implement a proximal gradient step on a meta-learned task loss. Concretely, context (x,y) tokens are encoded into keys/values that parameterize a learnable energy; a small MLP head supplies a bias/initialization term (GD-β) and a proximal regularizer, so that one or two Hopfield-style attention updates approximate gradient descent in function space while avoiding the nonzero-mean prior error of attention-only ICL. We train ES-ICL with a bilevel objective aligning the Hopfield energy gradient with the true gradient on held-out query tokens, and allocate heads to specialize to different examples/tasks to exploit multihead memorization capacity; at scale we replace softmax with linear attention to preserve the recurrent update view and enable long contexts. We hypothesize ES-ICL yields more stable, sample-efficient ICL and better OOD generalization by coupling associative retrieval with explicitly learned optimization dynamics.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability limitations of Neural Theorem Provers (NTPs), which are neuro-symbolic models that learn interpretable logical rules but must enumerate all possible proof paths, making them computationally infeasible for large problems. The key insight is that instead of exhaustively considering every proof path, a model can learn a conditional rule-selection strategy that focuses on the most promising rules for a given goal, enabling efficient end-to-end differentiable proving. The authors introduce Conditional Theorem Provers (CTPs), which augment NTPs with a learned, gradient-trained controller that selects candidate rules during backward-chaining proofs, preserving differentiability and interpretability while drastically reducing search complexity. Empirically, CTPs scale to larger reasoning tasks, achieve state-of-the-art generalization on CLUTRR for systematic extrapolation from small to large graphs, and improve link-prediction performance versus other neural-symbolic baselines.

result.text: Visual prompt tuning still lacks spatial selectivity, causing object and context evidence to tangle and degrade transfer under domain shift and fine-grained recognition. args.text: We propose Mirror-Descent Attention: unify attention-as-Hopfield-memory with in-context learning-as-optimization by interpreting each attention layer as a proximal/mirror-descent step on a context-defined energy. Concretely, replace softmax with a learned Bregman projection whose convex potential is parameterized from keys/values, so the update acts as one step of proximal functional gradient descent toward targets implicit in in-context pairs; across layers this yields unrolled optimization where early layers do entropy-regularized averaging and later layers sharpen into task-specific attractors via learned curvature. This enables non-linear ICL without extra MLPs by endowing each head with a "curvature potential" (and optional low-rank Newton-like corrections) that adapts the metric to the task. When the potential is quadratic, the update admits kernel feature maps and linear-time computation akin to linear transformers, predicting better stability/sample-efficiency than softmax while matching GD-β estimators on nonzero-mean priors.

We propose Diffusion Goal Distance (DGD): an action-free pretraining objective that learns a soft shortest-path reachability metric D(s, g) from unlabeled videos, then uses it to guide hierarchical goal-conditioned RL. Concretely, we build a spatiotemporal kNN graph over video embeddings and train D via a contrastive random-walk objective with absorbing goals plus a compositionality prior (D(s, g) ≈ min_h D(s, h) + D(h, g)), yielding a policy-similarity-aware goal metric that approximates goal-conditioned value without actions. At finetune time, we plug D into a HIQL-style decomposition as both a shaping potential and a high-level subgoal selector that greedily decreases D, then align it with true values via a lightweight contrastive-RL loss on (state, action, goal) tuples. This unifies action-free video pretraining with value-consistent, behaviorally grounded representations, targeting long-horizon, sparse-reward, image-based tasks where accurate Q estimates are brittle.

We propose Calibrated Residual-Uncertainty Triaging (CRUT) for unsupervised domain-adaptive object detection, which fuses category-specific reconstruction residuals with a probabilistic teacher’s predictive uncertainty to produce calibrated per-box quality scores. Per-class source dictionaries yield residual-based pseudo-IoU estimates, while a slowly-updated teacher provides uncertainty; a lightweight calibrator trained with a task-aware calibration loss on source and adapted to target via split-conformal adjustment converts these signals into reliable quality that guides learning. High-quality boxes drive self-training, medium-quality regions trigger class-conditional feature alignment via conditional kernels, and low-quality/ambiguous tiles are used for localized adversarial alignment, unifying robust pseudo supervision with context-aware alignment. This calibrated triaging reduces negative transfer, improves confidence reliability, and yields stronger cross-domain detection than using residuals or uncertainty alone.

The paper addresses the vulnerability of aligned open-source large language models to “jailbreak” attacks that induce harmful or unintended behavior despite pre-release alignment efforts. Its key insight is that many jailbreaks can be triggered not by exotic adversarial prompts but simply by exploiting the model’s decoding/generation process—varying sampling methods and decoding hyperparameters dramatically increases misalignment. The authors demonstrate a generation-exploitation attack that, across 11 popular models (LLaMA2, Vicuna, Falcon, MPT, etc.), raises the misalignment rate from 0% to over 95% with far lower computational cost than prior attacks, and they propose a defensive alignment approach that trains or evaluates models across diverse generation strategies to meaningfully reduce vulnerability.

result.text: The paper addresses limitations of visual prompt tuning (VPT)—notably poor initialization, sensitivity to prompt length, and weak performance when adapting self-supervised pretrained vision models to downstream tasks—and seeks a lightweight way to boost adaptation without full fine-tuning. Methodologically, the authors propose Self-Prompt-Tuning (SPT): compute prototype tokens from downstream data, initialize and optionally refine a small set of learnable prompt tokens based on these prototypes, and use a streamlined optimization pipeline that keeps compute overhead negligible compared to VPT; extensive experiments show SPT outperforms prior prompt and full fine-tuning on many benchmarks while using <0.4% of parameters and substantially improves adaptation for self-supervised pretrained models.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of large-scale, egocentric datasets that combine accurate 3D camera geometry with annotated video understanding for neural rendering and dynamic scene modeling. Its key insight is that augmenting an existing action-rich egocentric video corpus (EPIC-KITCHENS) with reconstructed camera poses and geometry removes the costly photogrammetry bottleneck and better supports tasks that require both spatial structure and semantic labels. The authors introduce EPIC Fields, a dataset that registers 19M frames across 45 kitchens (recovering cameras for 96% of videos) and pairs these 3D-enabled videos with action segments and VISOR object masks, and they demonstrate the utility by proposing methods and strong baselines for neural rendering and dynamic object segmentation that reveal current limitations and show geometry improves semi-supervised segmentation.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of consensus and conversion difficulty between LayerNorm (LN) and RMSNorm in Transformer architectures, where RMSNorm is cheaper but thought to reduce representational power compared to LN. The key insight is that the mean component removed by Pre-LN is redundant in the main residual branch, so by explicitly compressing or eliminating this zero-mean information one can reduce LN to an RMS-style normalization without loss of arithmetic functionality. The authors introduce Compressed RMSNorm (CRMSNorm) and corresponding Pre-CRMSNorm Transformers that perform a lossless compression of zero-mean vectors and prove formal equivalence between Pre-LN, Pre-RMSNorm, and Pre-CRMSNorm during training and inference, enabling direct substitution. Empirically, replacing Pre-LN with Pre-(C)RMSNorm yields identical behavior while cutting training and inference time by about 1%–10%.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of learning near-optimal predictive models when deploying a model changes the data distribution (performative prediction) and the learner must both collect feedback and minimize cumulative regret. The key insight is that performative feedback—observing samples from the induced shifted distribution after each deployment—yields a richer signal than standard bandit feedback, allowing regret to scale with the complexity of distribution shifts rather than the complexity of the reward function. The authors propose an algorithm that, under only smoothness assumptions on the shifts (no convexity needed), carefully explores to learn the mapping from models to induced distributions and constructs novel confidence bounds on unexplored models’ risks; this yields regret guarantees and ensures the final iterate is near-optimal. More broadly, their approach adapts bandit-style tools to exploit performative feedback for efficient regret minimization.

args.text: We propose Prototype-Subgoal GCRL: pretrain a prototypical dictionary over visual observations from large, action-free videos using bootstrap/temporal self-supervision, then refine it with a policy-similarity/bisimulation regularizer so prototypes group states by controllable, dynamics-relevant behavior. Building on hierarchical offline goal-reaching, a high-level policy plans in prototype space by predicting short sequences of target prototypes, while a low-level controller is trained via contrastive goal-conditioned value learning to drive the agent to any state within the chosen prototype cluster. To stabilize under sparse rewards and distractors, we constrain latent norms during pretraining and add a small predictive-information bonus, yielding dynamics-predictive yet compact embeddings. This prototype-space planning is expected to improve long-horizon success and cross-domain visual generalization over prior prototype and hierarchical methods.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection, aiming to transfer detector performance from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain while avoiding negative transfer from imperfect feature alignment. Its key insight is that learning category-specific dictionaries from source-domain object proposals lets target proposals be represented per-category, and the reconstruction residuals provide a reliable signal both for assigning pseudo-labels and estimating box quality (e.g., IoU), avoiding reliance on brittle global feature alignment or softmax decision boundaries. The method builds category dictionaries from source proposals, computes residuals for target candidate boxes to guide pseudo-box selection and weight their contribution by residual-derived quality scores, and trains the detector in a residual-weighted self-training loop that implicitly aligns domains and yields more informative, trustworthy pseudo-labels for improved cross-domain detection.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of diffusion-based offline planners whose performance and generalization are constrained by insufficient diversity of training data, especially for adapting to unseen goal-conditioned tasks. The key insight is to turn diffusion planning into an adaptive, self-evolving loop that generates synthetic expert-like trajectories guided by reward gradients and then filters those trajectories to iteratively improve the diffusion model, thereby enhancing planning quality and transfer to new tasks. Concretely, AdaptDiffuser uses reward-gradient-guided sampling to produce diverse candidate trajectories, applies a discriminator to select high-quality synthetic data, and finetunes the diffusion model on this curated data in a cyclical evolution process; experiments on Maze2D, MuJoCo, and a KUKA task show substantial gains over prior diffusion planners and improved adaptation to unseen tasks without extra expert data.

result.text: Transformation-Invariant Refusal (TIR) is a lightweight, model-agnostic guardrail that tests whether a candidate response remains safe across a bank of semantics-preserving obfuscation/normalization transforms tuned to known jailbreak channels. Building on the repeat-to-detect insight, TIR applies repeat/regenerate checks not only to the raw output but also to variants produced by unicode/homoglyph normalization, paraphrase and back-translation, and cipher-decoding via shadow decoders that target ciphered or non-standard character encodings seen in cipher-based and guardrail-evading attacks. The defense flags an answer if any transformed variant (or its repeat) reveals harmful content or if refusals are non-invariant across variants, catching output-filter evasions and token-level triggers that elude single-view detectors. We hypothesize substantially lower false negatives on guardrail-triggering and token-trigger benchmarks at modest query cost, without white-box access or fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper addresses false-positive errors in zero-shot segmentation that arise because CLIP, trained with image-level supervision, is insensitive to different mask proposals and thus gives similar classifications to many masks in the same image. args.text: We propose Geo-DeAOT, a geometry-aware dual-branch propagation framework for semi-supervised egocentric VOS that anchors object-agnostic features in world coordinates using recovered camera poses, while keeping object-specific propagation in the image domain. A differentiable unprojection/reprojection memory stabilizes the agnostic branch across rapid head motion and long occlusions, and a hand–object relation prior gates the specific branch to emphasize actively manipulated objects and resolve depth-order flips. Trained on 3D-registered egocentric video with VISOR masks, Geo-DeAOT reduces drift and preserves long-term object persistence without sacrificing efficiency via single-head gated updates and sparse 3D memory. This bridges geometry-enabled egocentric video with HOI-rich segmentation and should set new baselines on VISOR-style VOS protocols.

We propose Feature-Aware Post-Training Co-Compression (FAPC): first learn per-layer low-rank activation bases in an unsupervised, few-shot manner and project each linear layer’s outputs onto these bases; then run Fisher-guided structured pruning directly in the compressed feature space, jointly tuning small reconstruction adapters to preserve projected outputs. By aligning pruning decisions with the empirically low-rank structure of activations, FAPC reduces the mask search space and reconstruction burden, enabling larger FLOPs/latency reductions with minimal accuracy loss and no labeled data. A layerwise pipeline followed by a brief global fine-tune on unlabeled samples yields practical speedups on BERT/ViT while maintaining downstream performance, and transfers across tasks via re-estimated activation bases. We expect FAPC to outperform pure post-training pruning at equal accuracy and to improve upon activation-only compression by leveraging structure-aware sparsification in the compressed domain.

args.text: We propose a preconditioned kernel-Hopfield in-context learner that unifies linear-time attention with the associative-memory view to implement curvature-aware, one- to few-step optimization from context. A Transformer block with linear attention learns task-adaptive kernel features and uses an MLP to infer a low-rank preconditioner and prior mean from the prompt, so the associative KV accumulators perform a preconditioned GD-β update toward the Bayesian posterior; with non-linear kernels, this becomes a functional-gradient step while retaining linear-time complexity. A meta-objective trains the block to minimize posterior risk over task families, while the Hopfield energy perspective provides a convergence regularizer and layerwise step-size control. This design improves stability on long contexts and sample efficiency over plain linear-attention ICL, and extends naturally to non-linear tasks via learned kernels.

The method combines latent dynamics modeling with unsupervised goal-conditioned RL to pretrain an encoder from diverse, task-aligned observations, then finetunes this encoder with only 100k environment steps on Atari, showing strong gains over prior offline-pretraining baselines and competitive performance with much larger pretraining regimes. The approach scales favorably with larger models and more diverse observational data, approaching human-level performance and data-efficiency in the best settings.

result.text: The paper reframes reinforcement learning as a sequence modeling problem and addresses the challenge of producing high-return action sequences without relying on value-function estimation or policy-gradient optimization. The key insight is that a causally masked Transformer can be conditioned on past states, past actions, and a target return to autoregressively generate future actions that achieve that return, leveraging the scalability and simplicity of large-scale sequence models. Their method, Decision Transformer, concatenates returns-to-go, states, and actions into tokens and trains a Transformer to predict the next action given this conditioned trajectory; at test time the model autoregressively samples actions conditioned on a desired return to control an agent. Across offline benchmarks (Atari, OpenAI Gym, Key-to-Door) this simple conditional sequence-modeling approach matches or exceeds prior model-free offline RL baselines.

result.text: We propose Repeat-and-Decode (RaD), a black-box safeguard that extends repetition-based detection by asking the same LLM to first verbatim-repeat a candidate output and then restate its semantic content in plain natural language before any classification, flagging the sample if the restatement triggers refusal or reveals unsafe intent. By keeping the model in its natural generation channel (repeat → explain), RaD preserves alignment like repetition-only defenses while forcing ciphered or obfuscated outputs to be self-decoded, directly targeting output-filter evasion via non-standard characters and non-natural-language prompts. RaD yields a consistency score between the repeated text and the self-decoded explanation (and refusal tokens), improving recall on cipher/output-layer bypasses without inflating false positives. We will evaluate RaD on JAMBench and CipherChat settings and stress-test with automated attack generators (e.g., TAP) to measure gains over repeat-only baselines.

result.text: EgoDistill tackles the problem of making egocentric video understanding models feasible for resource-constrained settings by dramatically reducing their computational cost. The key insight is that rich clip-level video features produced by heavy models can be reconstructed by distilling semantics from a few sparsely sampled frames and complementary head-motion signals derived from lightweight IMU sensors, so expensive per-frame dense processing can be avoided. The method trains a student network to mimic heavy video-model features by fusing sparse visual embeddings with IMU-derived motion features, and introduces a self-supervised objective to learn robust IMU representations; at inference the student replaces the heavyweight model, yielding similar recognition accuracy with roughly 200× fewer GFLOPs.

args.text: I propose LR-Cache: augment layer-caching for diffusion transformers with low-rank activation reconstruction instead of pure reuse. For layers selected to skip, we store a reference activation and apply a per-layer, timestep-conditioned low-rank projector that predicts a small delta to the cached output from cheap inputs (e.g., timestep embedding and shallow features), learned post-training on a small unlabeled set to match original layer outputs. This adds an “approximate” mode to the cache router, enabling more aggressive skipping while preserving quality, with per-layer adaptive ranks and negligible extra FLOPs. A brief, layerwise reconstruction phase calibrates the low-rank bases and deltas, analogous to fast post-training output reconstruction, but targeting activation subspaces rather than masks.

result.text: The paper tackles source-free object detection, where a detector trained on a labeled source domain must be adapted to an unlabeled target domain without access to source data, a setting where noisy pseudo-labels from the source model degrade adaptation. Its key insight is that target samples can be split into source-similar and source-dissimilar subsets based on a detection-variance criterion—higher detection variance correlates with higher recall and greater similarity to the source—and that adversarially aligning these subsets in feature space reduces noise and improves pseudo supervision. The method implements this by computing detection variance to partition the target data, then embedding an adversarial discriminator into a mean teacher framework to make the feature distributions of the two subsets indistinguishable while leveraging the teacher’s pseudo-labels for training. Experiments across multiple cross-domain detection benchmarks show consistent gains over prior source-free adaptation approaches.

args.text: We propose PSM-from-Video Hierarchical Pretraining: learn a policy-similarity–aligned latent space from action-free videos, then use it for hierarchical goal-conditioned control. We first pretrain a latent world model on raw video and derive a policy-similarity proxy by aligning distributions over predicted futures (successor-like rollouts), yielding a representation that approximates PSM/bisimulation without rewards or actions. Clustering this space produces subgoal landmarks; a high-level policy selects latent subgoals while a low-level controller is trained via a contrastive RL objective where inner products implement goal-conditioned values. result.text: The paper tackles efficient compression of Transformer models for resource-constrained deployment, noting that prior weight-focused low-rank approximations perform poorly for transformers and require large labeled datasets to fine-tune. Its key insight is that activations (features) in transformer layers are empirically low-rank even though the learned weight matrices are not, so compressing outputs rather than weights yields more faithful reduction. Building on this, the authors introduce AAFM, which adaptively determines per-layer compression structure and locally compresses each linear layer's output features in a few-shot, unsupervised manner, followed by a global fine-tuning stage GFM that holistically optimizes the compressed network; both stages use only a small unlabeled sample set. The method achieves substantial parameter and latency reductions with minimal accuracy loss (e.g., 33% parameters removed and 18.8% throughput gain with only 0.23% ImageNet accuracy drop using 2K unlabeled images), transfers to NLP tasks, and generalizes well to downstream tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses safe linear stochastic bandits where, at each round, the learner must satisfy an unknown linear baseline constraint—i.e., ensure instantaneous reward stays above a given lower bound—while still maximizing cumulative reward. The key insight is that stage-wise conservatism can be enforced with modest impact on learning by designing conservative variants of Thompson Sampling and UCB that maintain confidence-aware safety while preserving near-optimal regret. Concretely, the authors propose SCLTS and SCLUCB algorithms that use linear model estimates and safety-aware action selection rules to ensure the baseline constraint with high probability, achieving regret bounds O(√T log^{3/2}T) and O(√T log T) respectively, and they show these methods extend with simple modifications to bandit-feedback constraints, unknown baseline actions, and upper-bound safety constraints while significantly reducing the number of baseline plays compared to prior work.

args.text: We propose Energy-Integrated ICL, a Transformer variant that treats each block as an ODE step of gradient flow on a Hopfield-style attention energy, explicitly integrating this flow across layers with a small fixed number of Runge-Kutta steps. The energy gradient is estimated with gated linear attention to yield linear-time, streaming updates over very long contexts, while a lightweight MLP bias path implements learnable priors (nonzero-mean) so the flow realizes one-step GD-β and its preconditioned extensions. We meta-learn per-head step sizes and preconditioners so the induced kernel matches the task distribution, making the dynamics approximate functional (natural) gradient descent in context and unifying associative retrieval with learned optimization. This design aims to achieve near-Bayes-optimal in-context regression on long sequences and improved nonlinear ICL stability, at subquadratic cost.

We propose Affordance-Conditioned Subtrajectory Diffusion: a diffusion planner that generates multi-step action-state sequences conditioned not only on the goal (and optional return) but also on a compact affordance embedding given by the vector of values of a library of low-level skills at the current state. By conditioning in this Value Function Space, the sampler preferentially stitches subtrajectories that are compositionally feasible with respect to available skills, improving long-horizon reliability over scalar value- or goal-only conditioning. We further employ a self-evolving improvement loop where reward/affordance gradients guide sampling and a feasibility discriminator filters candidates before finetuning the model, yielding progressively better stitching from offline data. At test time, the planner generalizes to new goals by searching over target affordance vectors (skill-weight profiles) and sampling plans that realize those targets, then executing or refining them with model-based control.

result.text: The paper tackles 3D visual grounding, where models must localize objects in 3D scenes from referential language, and asks whether richer 2D-like object cues can be synthesized from point clouds to improve 3D visual representations without extra 2D inputs. The key insight is that synthetic 2D views rendered from point clouds provide complementary, discriminative appearance and context information that can be distilled into the 3D encoder to strengthen its features for language-guided localization. Their method, Look Around and Refer (LAR), generates multiple synthetic 2D clues from each 3D proposal, extracts 2D features and uses a knowledge distillation framework to transfer those semantics into the 3D stream during training (and efficiently leverage them at test time), leading to consistent gains over prior state-of-the-art on Nr3D, Sr3D, and ScanRefer.

result.text: The paper investigates whether safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) holds when users communicate in non-natural languages (ciphers), addressing the risk that current defenses—trained primarily on natural language—may be bypassed. The key insight is that LLMs can understand and respond to ciphered prompts, and in fact exhibit a latent "secret cipher" behavior that can be triggered via role play and enciphered demonstrations, enabling stealthy jailbreaks even against strong models like GPT-4. The authors introduce CipherChat, a framework that sends system-role descriptions and few-shot enciphered examples to LLMs to systematically evaluate 11 safety domains across English and Chinese, showing that many human-designed ciphers and the proposed SelfCipher can nearly completely bypass GPT-4’s safety in several domains. Their results reveal a pressing need to extend alignment methods beyond natural languages and provide code and data for reproducibility.

args.text: I propose an in-context EM Transformer that replaces gradient-descent-style ICL with a learned, linear-time EM-like procedure using gated linear attention. Concretely, GLA heads produce token-to-component responsibilities, a linear-attention pass aggregates component-wise sufficient statistics, and a lightweight MLP performs a learned M-step update per component—recovering GD-β behavior within each cluster while handling multi-modal priors. Stacking a few such blocks yields several EM iterations in-context and scales to very long contexts due to the linear-time kernel. This should outperform GD-based ICL on mixture-of-linear-regressions and few-shot clustering, with mechanistic signatures of head/component specialization and gates approximating posterior responsibilities.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised domain-adaptive object detection, where self-training relies on noisy pseudo boxes from unlabeled target data and prior work neglects their uncertainty. The key insight is to model and leverage the teacher model’s evolving uncertainty instead of hard-thresholding pseudo labels, using uncertainty-guided consistency to adapt both classification and localization (and treating anchors as learnable parameters to adapt in parallel). Methodologically, they introduce a Probabilistic Teacher framework that estimates uncertainty from a slowly-updated teacher to guide a student via consistency losses, augment localization adaptation with anchor adaptation, and propose an Entropy Focal Loss to weight training by uncertainty; this combination yields substantial gains and new state-of-the-art results.

args.text: We propose diffusion-guided probabilistic path reasoning for incomplete knowledge graphs, framing multi-hop inference as conditional generation of diverse path sets given a query. A diffusion model over relation/entity sequences is trained on offline KG walks, then guided at sampling time by gradients from a BetaE-style query energy to handle conjunction/union/negation while adding an uncertainty bonus à la GaussianPath to avoid premature exploitation on sparse graphs. Soft rule priors from a learned rule generator are injected as masks or auxiliary energies so generation respects interpretable structure, and the sampled paths are aggregated into answer distributions akin to random-walk aggregation, yielding calibrated probabilities and rationales. This hybrid aims to combine coverage and logical expressivity of probabilistic embeddings with the diversity and controllability of diffusion, improving robustness and interpretability under KG incompleteness.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of egocentric video understanding methods that rely on short clip-level visual features and therefore fail to capture the camera-wearer’s broader, persistent environment and unseen local surroundings. The key insight is that training models to predict and encode the latent, human-centric environment from first-person video—using simulated 3D environments where full observability provides supervisory signal—yields environment-aware representations that transfer to real-world egocentric footage. The method trains on videos of agents in simulated scenes to learn features predictive of the local, potentially occluded environment and then plugs those learned representations into downstream human-centric video tasks; this yields consistent improvements over clip-only features and, despite simulation-only training, strong performance on real-world datasets including state-of-the-art results on the Ego4D NLQ challenge.

The paper tackles safe reinforcement learning in finite-horizon constrained Markov decision processes with unknown transitions, where an agent must learn to maximize reward while ensuring per-episode safety constraints on expected cumulative costs are never violated. The key insight is to jointly use optimism for reward-driven exploration and pessimism for constraint satisfaction—specifically combining a reward exploration bonus and a conservative (pessimistic) treatment of safety constraints on top of an optimistic model-based estimate of transitions—to balance learning efficiency with strict safety. The proposed algorithm, DOPE (Doubly Optimistic and Pessimistic Exploration), builds confidence sets for transition models, computes optimistic policies for rewards while imposing pessimistic constraints via conservative cost estimates, and uses the reward bonus to guide exploration; this yields a provable objective regret of Õ(|S|√(|A|K)) without any safety violations during learning and empirically outperforms prior optimism-pessimism methods.

result.text: We propose PSM-from-Video Hierarchical Pretraining: learn a policy-similarity–aligned latent space from action-free videos, then use it for hierarchical goal-conditioned control. We first pretrain a latent world model on raw video and derive a policy-similarity proxy by aligning distributions over predicted futures (successor-like rollouts), yielding a representation that approximates PSM/bisimulation without rewards or actions. Clustering this space produces subgoal landmarks; a high-level policy selects latent subgoals while a low-level controller is trained via a contrastive RL objective where inner products implement goal-conditioned values. This combination targets long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks and improves zero-shot generalization under visual distractions.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap in evaluating and attacking moderation guardrails in large language models (LLMs), noting that many jailbreak benchmarks ignore prompts that trigger input- or output-level moderation filters; this leaves both evaluation and red-teaming incomplete. The key insight is that effective jailbreaks must target both input filters (via crafted prefixes) and output filters (by encoding harmful content using non-standard “cipher characters” produced by a surrogate model that mimics the guardrail), enabling harmful content to evade detection and decoding back into readable form. The authors introduce JAMBench, a 160-instruction benchmark spanning four risk categories and multiple severity levels designed to reliably trigger guardrails, and propose JAM, a two-part attack combining jailbreak prefixes to bypass input-level defenses with a fine-tuned shadow model that generates cipher-character outputs to slip past output-level filters; experiments on four LLMs show JAM substantially increases jailbreak success and reduces filtering compared to baselines.

Its key insight is that explicitly modeling and transferring multi-level visual concepts into the textual prompt space yields stronger alignment between vision and language and improves generalization across domains. The proposed Concept-Guided Prompt Learning (CPL) builds a visual concept cache from pretrained CLIP features and uses a learned projector to transform multi-level visual features into text-feature-like embeddings that guide prompt generation, producing concept-aware prompts that enhance visual–linguistic consistency. Experiments show CPL substantially outperforms state-of-the-art prompt tuning methods on generalization benchmarks, especially for fine-grained datasets.

args.text: Render-to-Align: learn cross-view, fine-grained egocentric action representations by synthesizing exocentric viewpoints with geometry-aware neural rendering, then aligning to unpaired exocentric videos using object-centric, audio-anchored contrastive learning. Leveraging EPIC Fields’ recovered camera poses, we perform short-horizon dynamic view synthesis to generate "orbit" clips around hands and active objects, using VISOR masks to focus supervision on hand–object regions. We then apply an AE2-style temporal alignment objective with reversed-time negatives between the synthesized exocentric clips and real, unpaired exocentric footage, while sampling around audio-indicated interaction moments to emphasize state-changing events. This produces effectively paired cross-view signals without multi-camera capture, improving cross-view transfer, HOI segmentation, and fine-grained action recognition in both ego and exo settings.

result.text: I propose LR-Cache: augment layer-caching for diffusion transformers with low-rank activation reconstruction instead of pure reuse. For layers selected to skip, we store a reference activation and apply a per-layer, timestep-conditioned low-rank projector that predicts a small delta to the cached output from cheap inputs (e.g., timestep embedding and shallow features), learned post-training on a small unlabeled set to match original layer outputs. This adds an “approximate” mode to the cache router, enabling more aggressive skipping while preserving quality, with per-layer adaptive ranks and negligible extra FLOPs. A brief, layerwise reconstruction phase calibrates the low-rank bases and deltas, analogous to fast post-training output reconstruction, but targeting activation subspaces rather than masks.

result.text: The paper addresses source data-free unsupervised domain adaptive object detection, where labeled source data cannot be accessed due to privacy or transmission constraints, so conventional UDA methods that jointly train on source and target are infeasible. The key insight is to recast SFOD as learning with noisy labels by using a source-pretrained detector to generate pseudo labels on the target and to automatically select a reliable confidence threshold via a proposed self-entropy descent (SED) metric, while recognizing and mitigating dominant false negatives in those pseudo labels. The method uses SED to find the threshold that yields low-entropy, trustworthy predictions, then simulates and mines false negatives through augmentation strategies (e.g., Mosaic) during target-only fine-tuning to recover missed objects, and demonstrates state-of-the-art results across multiple adaptation tasks without any source data.

result.text: MetaDiffuser addresses the problem of generalizing offline reinforcement learning across tasks with varying rewards or dynamics by casting meta-RL as a conditional trajectory-generation problem. The key insight is to treat task generalization as context-conditioned diffusion planning: learn a diffusion model that generates task-oriented trajectories conditioned on a contextual task representation, and guide sampling to ensure both high return and dynamics consistency. The method trains a context-conditioned diffusion model on offline meta-datasets and, at test time, uses a dual-guided sampling module—one guide encouraging high returns and another enforcing dynamics consistency—to produce trajectories for planning; this approach is robust to limited warm-start data and compatible with different task representations, outperforming strong baselines on MuJoCo.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised monocular depth estimation in dynamic scenes by explicitly modeling per-object 6-DoF motion together with camera ego-motion, addressing failures of prior methods that treat moving objects as outliers. Its key insight is that correctly handling object motion requires a geometrically accurate forward-projection formulation (not the common inverse projection) and that combining instance-aware photometric and geometric consistency yields stronger self-supervision for both background and object regions. The method implements a neural forward-projection module to render objects under estimated 6-DoF transforms, integrates a unified instance-aware consistency loss that enforces photometric and geometric alignment for each segmented instance, and leverages an auto-annotation pipeline using off-the-shelf instance segmentation and optical flow to produce video instance masks for training. Empirically, this end-to-end framework improves depth and motion estimation on KITTI and Cityscapes, outperforming prior state-of-the-art approaches.

The paper tackles the practical challenge of reducing Transformer inference cost without the high time and complexity of retraining-based pruning methods by proposing a fast post-training pruning framework. The key insight is that structured sparsity can be applied post-training if one carefully selects and adjusts masks to preserve important parameters—using Fisher-information-guided mask search, complementary mask rearrangement, and a lightweight mask-tuning step that reconstructs layer outputs. Their method automatically finds which heads and filters to remove under a resource constraint and applies only brief, layerwise reconstruction (no full retraining), enabling up to 2.0x FLOPs reduction and 1.56x latency speedup on BERT-base and DistilBERT with under 1% accuracy loss on GLUE and SQuAD. result.text: Extend object-identifier LLM grounding in 3D to a persistent 4D setting where the same real-world instance keeps a stable token across multiple scans of a scene. Its key insight is that tasks can form a Boolean algebra—closed under negation, conjunction, and disjunction—so that if an agent has learned appropriate goal-oriented value functions for a set of base tasks and transitions are suitably constrained, those value functions can be composed to produce optimal solutions for any Boolean combination of the bases. result.text: The paper addresses whether detecting adversarially perturbed inputs is fundamentally easier than correctly classifying them, aiming to understand limits of detector-based defenses. Its key insight is a hardness reduction showing that any detector robust to adversarial perturbations of radius r can be transformed (albeit with computational inefficiency) into a classifier robust to perturbations of radius r/2 without increasing sample complexity, implying that strong detection guarantees would already yield highly robust classifiers. Methodologically, the authors construct a theoretical reduction from detection to classification that preserves sample complexity but is computationally infeasible, and they apply this sanity-check to 14 published empirical detectors—finding that for 12 of them the reported detection claims would imply an implausibly powerful (inefficient) robust classifier, thereby casting doubt on those detection results.

result.text: We propose Calibrated Residual-Uncertainty Triaging (CRUT) for unsupervised domain-adaptive object detection, which fuses category-specific reconstruction residuals with a probabilistic teacher’s predictive uncertainty to produce calibrated per-box quality scores. Per-class source dictionaries yield residual-based pseudo-IoU estimates, while a slowly-updated teacher provides uncertainty; a lightweight calibrator trained with a task-aware calibration loss on source and adapted to target via split-conformal adjustment converts these signals into reliable quality that guides learning. result.text: The paper addresses the need to reduce manual, instance-specific prompts in promptable segmentation by transforming a single task-generic prompt into accurate instance-specific prompts without relying on perfect MLLM outputs. Its key insight is that MLLM "hallucinations"—usually treated as errors—encode useful, large-scale contextual knowledge that can be mined and then verified against image-derived masks to produce more precise prompts. The proposed method, ProMaC, pairs a prompt generator that uses multi-scale chain-of-thought prompting to deliberately elicit and then distill hallucinated context into candidate instance prompts with a mask generator that enforces mask semantic alignment; masks produced feed back to iteratively refine the prompt generator, suppress irrelevant hallucinations, and converge on better prompts and segmentation. Experiments on five benchmarks show this iterative Prompt-Mask Cycle improves prompt precision and segmentation performance.

args.text: We propose Diffusion-Proof Paths: a query-conditioned diffusion model that samples multi-hop relation sequences (latent rules) for knowledge-graph reasoning, replacing brittle combinatorial search with a distribution over proof paths. Sampling is dual-guided by gradients from a BetaE-style differentiable FOL satisfaction score and a KG-dynamics prior, while an EM-style loop selects high-quality sampled paths to train a conditional rule generator/selector. Maintaining uncertainty over path proposals mitigates premature exploitation in exploration, akin to Bayesian Q-learning for path finding. Inspired by adaptive diffusion planning, we iteratively self-generate and filter synthetic proof trajectories to continually refine both the sampler and the rule set, yielding interpretable rules that support conjunction/disjunction/negation on incomplete graphs.

Active 3D language grounding via query-conditioned next-best-view planning: treat the set of object identifier tokens as competing hypotheses and select a short sequence of sensor poses that maximally reduces referential uncertainty. We estimate information gain by projecting language-conditioned spatial attention over pairwise 3D relations onto a view-consistent feature field distilled from vision–language models, rendering synthetic glimpses to score candidate poses without physical motion. During training, multi-view 2D cues rendered around proposals are distilled back into the 3D encoder to sharpen query-aware features, and evaluation simulates viewpoint budgets on hierarchical, ambiguous queries. This yields efficient disambiguation of fine-grained referents and robust grounding under occlusion and clutter.

result.text: The paper addresses the vulnerability of aligned large language models (LLMs) to adversarial "jailbreak" prompts that attempt to bypass safety guardrails, proposing a detection mechanism to distinguish malicious queries from benign ones. The key insight is that the model’s refusal loss—how strongly it resists producing harmful content—exhibits distinctive landscape properties (both in scalar values and smoothness of gradients) for jailbreak prompts versus normal queries. The authors introduce Gradient Cuff, a two-step detector that probes the refusal loss landscape by measuring functional refusal loss and gradient-based smoothness features around an input and then applies thresholding to flag likely jailbreaks. Experiments on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B-V1.5 across six jailbreak attack types show Gradient Cuff substantially increases rejection of malicious prompts while preserving acceptance of benign queries through adjustable thresholds.

The proposed Learning-to-Cache (L2C) method treats each transformer layer as a cacheable unit and learns an input-invariant but timestep-varying router via a differentiable optimization objective to decide which layers to reuse versus recompute, producing a static computation graph at deployment; experiments show L2C removes a large fraction of layer computations (e.g., up to ~94% in some cache steps) while preserving FID and outperforming existing samplers and prior cache methods at equal inference speed.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding and extending the transformer attention mechanism by linking it to associative memory: it asks what kind of memory model attention implements and how that explains transformers’ behavior and learning. The key insight is that transformer attention is exactly the update rule of a newly formulated modern Hopfield network with continuous states that can store an exponential number of patterns, converge rapidly (often in one update), and trade off storage capacity against convergence speed and retrieval error; this interpretation explains three types of energy minima (global averaging, metastable subset-averaging, and single-pattern fixed points) and how different transformer layers and attention heads operate and learn. Methodologically, the authors derive the Hopfield energy and update equations that match attention, analyze dynamics and gradients across layers (showing early layers favor global averaging while later layers form metastable attractors), demonstrate practical gains on tasks like immune-repertoire classification, and provide a PyTorch "Hopfield" layer and Gaussian-weighting simplification for replacing average-like heads to integrate this memory-attention perspective into deep architectures.

args.text: We propose an active KG reasoning system that answers arbitrary FOL queries by combining probabilistic embedding-based inference with uncertainty-aware exploration. Entities and queries are represented as Beta distributions and composed via learned logical operators to produce a soft posterior over answers; a complementary RL agent treats KG traversal and edge-probing as actions and selects informative relations/paths to reduce the posterior’s entropy under a query-specific budget. This yields budgeted, interactive query answering on incomplete KGs while uncovering supporting paths and candidate rules as byproducts.
