result.text: The paper tackles open-world object detection, where a detector must recognize known classes, discover unknown objects, and incrementally learn new categories without forgetting. The key insight is to impose a semantic topology that assigns all instances of a category—including an explicit “unknown” node—to consistent pre-defined nodes, which enforces discriminative features and stable inter-class relationships that both separate unknowns from knowns and prevent feature drift during incremental learning. Methodologically, the authors integrate this topology into the detector’s representation space (using either random graphs or language-model-derived semantic structures) so that training aligns instances to their category nodes, and show through extensive experiments that this unified constraint significantly reduces open-set errors and outperforms prior modular approaches.

The paper tackles the problem of implicit planning in reinforcement learning, specifically how to leverage value-iteration-like planners when environments are not given in tabular form and data is scarce. The key insight is that running planning computations on scalar value predictions per state creates an "algorithmic bottleneck" that harms data efficiency, and that performing planning instead in a high-dimensional latent space can preserve planning structure while avoiding this bottleneck. The authors introduce XLVINs, which learn a latent state representation and a graph-structured transition model, then execute value-iteration-like computation entirely in that latent space using neural graph-algorithmic modules trained with contrastive self-supervision so the latent planner aligns with true value iteration; this yields substantial data-efficiency gains across control, navigation, and Atari tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses safe constrained reinforcement learning: how to learn policies that maximize reward while satisfying constraints (e.g., safety or fairness). The key insight is to split each policy update into an unconstrained improvement step followed by a projection that explicitly enforces constraints, which yields provable bounds on reward improvement and constraint violation per update. The proposed method, Projection-Based Constrained Policy Optimization (PCPO), implements this two-step procedure and analyzes convergence when projecting under either L2 norm or KL divergence; experiments on control tasks show substantially reduced constraint violations and higher rewards compared to prior methods.

args.text: Entropy-Margin Coupled Attention (EMCA) adds a joint objective and parameterization that simultaneously preserves an entropy floor, induces max-margin token selection, and resists over-smoothing. Concretely, we reparameterize all projection layers with spectral-norm control to guarantee a provable lower bound on per-head attention entropy and Lipschitzness, and we add a margin-raising loss on attention-weighted value scores that explicitly separates top-k "optimal" tokens from the rest, matching the max-margin implicit bias of softmax attention. To avoid token uniformity while retaining beneficial low-rank structure, we couple this with a fidelity regularizer on attention outputs and a mild block nuclear-norm prior on latent features. We hypothesize this yields warmup-free stable training, deeper stacks, and improved long-context generalization across vision and language.

args.text: We propose Transformation-Certified Refusal (TCR), a test-time guardrail that provides deterministic certificates of refusal under a finite but expressive set of input/output obfuscations and decoding regimes. TCR composes a bank of canonicalizing input transforms and paraphrases with a self-decoding output audit (repeat→explain) to normalize ciphered responses, then applies a DSSN-style derandomized smoothing over a structured partition of the transform×decoding space to compute a provable lower bound on the prompt’s refusal probability. The system targets cipher/output-filter evasions and decoding-exploitation by flagging any cell that yields unsafe content while otherwise certifying a minimum refusal rate at fixed latency, enabling auditable safety dashboards and triage with guarantees. We will evaluate TCR against JAMBench ciphers and CipherChat prompts and stress-test with decoding-perturbation attacks to quantify certified coverage versus added latency.

result.text: The paper addresses improving prompt learning for large vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) by overcoming the limitation of single learned prompts and the collapse that occurs when multiple prompts are naively matched to the same visual feature. The key insight is to represent images and categories as sets of visual and textual features and to use optimal transport to flexibly match multiple learned prompts to diverse visual cues, preventing prompts from collapsing to a single point. Methodologically, the authors learn multiple prompts via a two-stage optimization: an inner loop computes an optimal transport alignment between visual features and prompts using the Sinkhorn algorithm, and an outer loop updates the prompt parameters to minimize this transport-based distance on supervised few-shot recognition data; experiments show consistent improvements over baselines.

args.text: Conservative performative exploration with baseline guarantees: maintain confidence sets over the mapping from model parameters to induced distributions and their performative risks, then deploy a candidate model only when its lower-confidence improvement over a known safe baseline exceeds a conservative budget; otherwise, default to the baseline. This CP-UCB-style rule yields high-probability bounds that keep cumulative excess performative risk over the baseline sublinear (or zero under checkpointed safety) while achieving regret that scales with the complexity of distributional shifts rather than the loss class. When the performative risk is convex under suitable structural assumptions, the scheme can further leverage targeted gradient estimates for faster rates. Analysis follows an optimism-for-reward/performative-risk with a conservative feasibility check, adapted to the performative feedback setting.

result.text: We propose PSM-from-Video Hierarchical Pretraining: learn a policy-similarity–aligned latent space from action-free videos, then use it for hierarchical goal-conditioned control. We first pretrain a latent world model on raw video and derive a policy-similarity proxy by aligning distributions over predicted futures (successor-like rollouts), yielding a representation that approximates PSM/bisimulation without rewards or actions. Clustering this space produces subgoal landmarks; a high-level policy selects latent subgoals while a low-level controller is trained via a contrastive RL objective where inner products implement goal-conditioned values. This combination targets long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks and improves zero-shot generalization under visual distractions.

result.text: We propose Open-Set Calibrated Triaging (OSCT) for domain-adaptive/source-free object detection, which estimates a per-box knownness by fusing category-dictionary reconstruction residuals with a probabilistic teacher’s predictive uncertainty and calibrates it via a task-aware calibrator adapted on target using split-conformal risk control. High-knownness boxes drive self-training; medium-knownness regions trigger localized adversarial/feature alignment; and low-knownness (likely-novel) boxes are masked from pseudo-labels and used only to train an abstention head and to support masked alignment, preventing negative transfer from unknown classes. The calibrator follows a TCD-style auxiliary calibration at source and is bootstrapped on target from teacher–student agreement, while residual cues provide class-conditional pseudo-IoU to disentangle mislocalized known objects from truly novel ones. OSCT improves AP on known classes and confidence reliability under open-set shift without requiring access to source data.

args.text: Successor-Feature-Guided Diffusion Planning: learn a trajectory diffusion model conditioned on a target cumulative feature vector (successor features) rather than only scalar return, and pair it with a learned convex coverage set (CCS) of policies in successor-feature space to enable zero-shot optimal transfer to any new linear reward. At inference, solve for the optimal target successor feature ψ* by maximizing w^Tψ over the CCS, then guide sampling with a feature-matching objective that penalizes deviation between the sampled trajectory’s predicted successor features and ψ*, optionally combining reward-gradient guidance for additional shaping—yielding stitched, in-distribution plans aligned with the optimal linear objective. Train by relabeling offline data with successor-feature estimates, and periodically expand the CCS frontier via self-evolving, reward-guided synthetic rollouts to cover missing regions in feature space. This unifies the optimality guarantees of SF-based transfer with the flexible stitching and generalization of diffusion planners for robust long-horizon control.

result.text: The paper addresses the under-explored challenge of spatial understanding in large language and vision-language models by introducing SpatialEval, a benchmark that tests relationship understanding, navigation, and counting. The key insight is that spatial reasoning remains hard—models sometimes perform worse than random—and surprisingly, adding visual input does not always help: VLMs can underperform pure LLMs and multi-modal models may ignore visual cues when strong textual hints exist. To probe these effects the authors systematically evaluate a range of competitive LLMs and VLMs on diverse spatial tasks and show that exploiting redundancy between text and vision can substantially improve performance, suggesting directions for building multimodal models with better spatial intelligence.

We propose Transformation-Certified Refusal (TCR), a test-time guardrail that provides deterministic certificates of refusal under a finite but expressive set of input/output obfuscations and decoding regimes. TCR composes a bank of canonicalizing input transforms and paraphrases with a self-decoding output audit (repeat→explain) to normalize ciphered responses, then applies a DSSN-style derandomized smoothing over a structured partition of the transform×decoding space to compute a provable lower bound on the prompt’s refusal probability. The system targets cipher/output-filter evasions and decoding-exploitation by flagging any cell that yields unsafe content while otherwise certifying a minimum refusal rate at fixed latency, enabling auditable safety dashboards and triage with guarantees. We will evaluate TCR against JAMBench ciphers and CipherChat prompts and stress-test with decoding-perturbation attacks to quantify certified coverage versus added latency.

result.text: The paper addresses the trade-off in self-supervised visual representation learning between producing global features suited for classification and local features suited for detection/segmentation. Its key insight is that a single model can learn both types of features by applying a variance-invariance-covariance regularization (VICReg) objective simultaneously at global and local levels, using geometric consistency to match corresponding local descriptors across differently distorted views. The method, VICRegL, feeds two augmented views through twin convolutional branches, applies the VICReg loss to pooled global embeddings, and also applies VICReg to pre-pooling local feature maps by pairing local vectors either when their L2 distance is below a threshold or when their relative positions align under the known geometric transform; this yields strong transfer performance on segmentation and competitive classification results.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that reinforcement learning agents trained on a few environments often fail to generalize to new, unseen environments by proposing a way to learn representations that capture behaviorally relevant structure. The key insight is a theoretically motivated policy similarity metric (PSM) that rates states as similar when the optimal policies at those states — and in their future trajectories — are alike, thereby encoding sequential and long-horizon behavioral equivalence rather than superficial observation similarity. Methodologically, the authors introduce a contrastive embedding procedure that can take any state similarity metric and produce representations that respect it, instantiate this with PSM to produce policy similarity embeddings (PSEs), and show empirically that PSEs improve generalization across several benchmarks including LQR with spurious correlations, a pixel-based jumping task, and the Distracting DM Control Suite.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of directed generation: producing samples with desired properties when only abundant unlabeled data and a smaller noisy reward-labeled dataset are available. The key insight is to use a learned reward predictor on the small labeled set as a pseudolabeler and train a conditional diffusion model to approximate the reward-conditioned data distribution, which both enables sampling toward target rewards and recovers a latent subspace representation of the data. Methodologically, the authors prove that this reward-directed conditional diffusion can learn and sample from the conditional distribution and that its reward improvement relative to the original data population is governed by an off-policy bandit-type regret in the learned feature subspace, with performance depending on reward signal strength, distribution shift, and extrapolation cost; they corroborate these theoretical findings with empirical experiments linking extrapolation strength to sample quality.

We propose Transformation-Invariant Refusal (TIR), a test-time guardrail that defends against input-layer jailbreaks by enforcing refusal consistency across a randomized ensemble of prompt transformations (e.g., paraphrases, Unicode/whitespace perturbations, transliteration/homoglyph swaps, and simple cipherings). TIR conducts short-prefix probes under this view distribution and estimates a binomial lower bound on the refusal probability; it flags or escalates when any unsafe variant appears or the certified refusal rate falls below a threshold, and pairs with a repeat-and-self-decode step to canonicalize obfuscated outputs before final judgment. This extends the randomized-smoothing perspective to input representations (complementary to decoding-invariant defenses), targeting cipher- and formatting-based bypasses without large latency via caching and lightweight paraphrase/perturbation generators. We will evaluate on JAMBench and CipherChat and study composition with decoding-invariant refusal to harden both input and output channels against black-box search attacks.

The key insight is that self-attention layers implicitly minimize a smoothness-promoting nonlocal functional, so preventing over-smoothing requires a regularizer that preserves fidelity between input tokens and the smoothed outputs. result.text: The paper addresses the theoretical gap in understanding how softmax attention in transformers learns to select important tokens despite its nonconvex training dynamics. The key insight is that gradient descent on the attention parameters converges in direction to a max-margin separator that discriminates locally-optimal tokens from non-optimal ones, thereby formalizing attention as an implicit margin-maximizing token selector whose notion of optimality is determined by value embeddings and problem geometry. Methodologically, the authors analyze the softmax-attention model f(X)=⟨Xv, softmax(XWp)⟩ and prove directional convergence results for gradient descent on p (and W), extend the analysis to regularization paths and nonlinear heads, and characterize joint v and p training under logistic loss as converging to coupled hard-margin SVM solutions influenced by each other’s support vectors. They validate these theoretical claims with numerical experiments that illustrate the predicted margin-maximizing behavior.

result.text: The paper tackles slow inference in diffusion transformers, where each denoising step executes a large transformer resulting in high computational cost. Its key insight is that many transformer layers produce redundant, timestep-repetitive computations that can be cached and skipped without modifying model weights, yielding large FLOPs and latency savings with negligible quality loss. The proposed Learning-to-Cache (L2C) method treats each transformer layer as a cacheable unit and learns an input-invariant but timestep-varying router via a differentiable optimization objective to decide which layers to reuse versus recompute, producing a static computation graph at deployment; experiments show L2C removes a large fraction of layer computations (e.g., up to ~94% in some cache steps) while preserving FID and outperforming existing samplers and prior cache methods at equal inference speed.

args.text: We propose a norm-certified, selective higher-order attention Transformer that enforces per-layer spectral-norm constraints and cosine/L2-style attention to keep Q, K, V entries within a provably bounded regime, certifying when near-linear triple-wise (tensor) attention can be safely invoked. Each layer maintains a cheap magnitude certificate; when satisfied it computes higher-order attention on token clusters suggested by the convex-dual low-rank bias, otherwise it falls back to stable linearized pairwise attention—thereby avoiding entropy collapse while preserving Lipschitzness. This design yields a certifiably stable, invertible-friendly architecture that selectively exploits higher-order correlations with n^{1+o(1)} cost on long contexts. We hypothesize improvements on tasks requiring ternary relations (e.g., coreference chains and program analysis) where pairwise attention underutilizes structure.

args.text: We propose conservative performative bandits: online model selection under performative distribution shift with a high-probability baseline-safety requirement that cumulative loss never falls more than a budget below a known baseline predictor. The method combines conservative action gating from conservative contextual bandits with performative-feedback modeling that locally estimates the distributional response (e.g., Jacobian) via targeted probes. We design an optimistic-performative UCB whose recommendation is executed only if a pessimistic bound on baseline-relative loss under the induced shift is satisfied, otherwise it defaults to the baseline. Under smooth performative maps and sub-Gaussian noise, this yields Õ(√T) regret to the performative optimum while ensuring sublinear cumulative safety violation (or zero with a strictly safe baseline), validated on strategic classification and auction bidding benchmarks.

We propose Entropy-Bounded Higher-Order Attention: a training-time control scheme for tensor (e.g., triple-wise) attention that maintains the bounded-entry regime enabling near-linear algorithms by combining per-head spectral normalization of Q/K/V with a learned temperature schedule that enforces a target attention-entropy floor per layer. By keeping tensor logits below the hardness threshold, the sketching-based n^{1+o(1)} procedure remains valid while simultaneously preventing attention-entropy collapse and depth-wise over-smoothing. We derive bounds linking spectral norms and temperature to tensor-logit magnitude and attention entropy, and implement an adaptive controller that tightens spectral scales or raises temperature when measured entropy drops below target. Experiments on long-context vision and language tasks show this unlocks practical higher-order attention with near-linear cost, stable training without warmup, and accuracy on par with or better than exact tensor attention.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised domain adaptation for object detection, where detectors trained on a source domain fail on target domains due to appearance, viewpoint, and background shifts, and where standard adversarial alignment or naive pseudo-labeling each have shortcomings. Its key insight is to use model predictive uncertainty to decide which target predictions should serve as reliable pseudo-labels and which should instead guide adversarial feature alignment via localized "tiles," thereby combining class-level supervision with context-aware alignment. The method quantifies uncertainty in class and bounding-box outputs, uses low-uncertainty predictions to self-train the detector, and uses high-uncertainty regions to create tiles for adversarial instance/image-level feature alignment, synergistically leveraging both signals during adaptation. Experiments across diverse domain shifts show this uncertainty-guided combination outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches.
